questions.q: Why does this lesson say 'a backup exists' and 'a backup works' are different claims?
options: Because file existence can't be checked with PowerShell
They are actually the same claim
A backup file can exist and be recent while still being corrupted or unrestorable — the only way to know for sure is to actually test it
Backups in Azure SQL never fail
questions.explain: Lesson 17's health check confirmed existence and recency; this lesson tests whether the backup actually restores cleanly.

options: Deletes old backups automatically
Only checks the backup file's size on disk
Restores the most recent backup to a temporary database, runs DBCC CHECKDB against it to verify integrity, then cleans up — a genuine end-to-end test
Only checks the backup's timestamp
questions.explain: This is a real restore-and-verify test, not a metadata check — exactly the gap between 'exists' and 'works.'

questions.q: What two results must both read 'Success' for a backup to count as verified?
options: RestoreResult and DbccResult
QueueDelay and GracePeriod
ServerName and DatabaseName
BackupDate and FileSize
questions.explain: RestoreResult confirms the backup restored; DbccResult confirms the restored copy isn't corrupted — both matter.

questions.q: What does running Test-OverlookBackup on a schedule actually change about Overlook's claim to leadership or a regulator?
options: It replaces the need for a failover group
It eliminates the need for any backups going forward
It turns 'we assume backups work' into 'we tested this specific backup today and it restored cleanly' — a materially more defensible answer
Nothing changes; it's the same assumption as before
questions.explain: Regular, scripted verification produces an actual tested result instead of an unverified assumption.

questions.q: How does backup verification connect to Lesson 11's RPO target?
options: RPO is only measured in dollars, not time
Backup verification replaces the need for an RPO target entirely
It doesn't connect; RPO only applies to the failover group

A verified, restorable backup is one half of what the RPO target depends on for the backup/restore recovery path — an RPO target is meaningless if the backup it assumes exists doesn't actually restore
questions.explain: The RPO target assumes a usable backup/restore path exists; verification is what actually confirms that assumption holds.
